### Construction of plasmids and strains
The strains and plasmids used in this work are shown in Tables 1 and 2 . The MSS11 gene fragment was amplified by PCR using the specific primers MSS11 -U (5′-GGGCCCGAATTCGATACCGAATCACGAAGG-3′) and MSS11 -D (5′-GGGCCCGAATTCATAGTGTCACTGGCACCC-3′) with the genomic DNA of S. cerevisiae W303-1A as template. After Eco RI digestion, the fragment was ligated with YCplac22 vector (Gietz and Sugino 1988 ) by T 4 DNA ligase to successfully construct recombinant plasmid YCplac22- MSS11 .
Open in a new tab YCplac22 (control) and YCplac22- MSS11 (experimental group) were transformed into W303-1A and JT139 strains respectively by lithium acetate transformation. Successful transformants were selected on CM-Trp medium and verified by colony PCR. The primers MSS11 -U and MSS11 -D were designed to anneal within the MSS11
ORF itself. Crucially, this amplicon is present on both the chromosomal locus and the recombinant plasmid YCplac22- MSS11 . Therefore, a positive PCR signal confirms the presence of the MSS11 sequence in the cell but does not distinguish its genomic location. To unambiguously confirm the presence of the plasmid, we performed an additional control: only strains harboring the YCplac22-based plasmid (either empty or containing MSS11 ) can grow on CM-Trp medium, which provides direct phenotypic evidence of successful transformation. The specific overexpression of the MSS11 gene from the plasmid in the engineered strains was subsequently quantified and confirmed by real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis (Fig. 1 ), which measures the total MSS11 expression level and showed a significant increase in Eng-1 and Eng-3 compared to their respective controls

### Fermentation conditions and product determination
The fermentation process was conducted in three stages. First, an appropriate number of cells from the CM-Trp solid medium was inoculated into 5 ml of CM-Trp liquid medium for activation. After 2∼4 h, the cells were transferred into 45 ml of CM-Trp medium and incubated overnight at 30°C with continuous shaking at 200 rpm. Subsequently, the cells were inoculated into 100 ml of YPD medium for high-density fermentation, with the initial OD 600nm adjusted to 0.5. The initial glucose concentration was 40 g/l (4%(w/v)). During fermentation, samples were collected every 2 h to monitor cell growth and glucose consumption. Ethanol content in the fermentation broth was measured starting from the 10-h time point.
In the aforementioned shake flask fermentation experiment, microaerophilic conditions were employed. Add 100 milliliters of culture medium to a 250-ml fermentation flask, inoculate the culture, and then tightly sealed with aluminum foil (ensuring no gaps and allowing only minimal gas exchange). The fermentation bottles were then incubated in a shaking incubator at 30°C and 200 rpm. The initial air inside the shaking flasks was rapidly consumed during yeast growth and metabolism (especially during the initial aerobic respiration phase), while the tight sealing with aluminium foil significantly reduced the entry of external oxygen. After 6–8 h of fermentation, a low-oxygen environment gradually formed, thereby meeting the requirements for microaerobic fermentation.

### Transcriptomic sequencing
Transcriptome analysis is a comprehensive study of all transcriptional products within cells under specific conditions, primarily including mRNA, non-coding RNA, and other RNA species. In S. cerevisiae , transcriptome analysis is typically conducted using high-throughput sequencing technologies, such as RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). The main procedural steps are as follows: First, total RNA is extracted from yeast cells, and its concentration, purity, and integrity are assessed. The RNA is then fragmented and reverse transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA). Sequencing adapters are subsequently added to the cDNA, and the samples are sequenced using platforms such as Illumina HiSeq X Ten (San Diego, CA, USA). Finally, the sequencing data are processed through alignment, quantification, and differential expression analysis to identify and interpret transcriptional changes.
Transcriptome perturbations were analyzed for Eng-0 and Eng-1 strains. Eng-0 served as a control. Two RNA-Seq repeats were performed. Samples were collected for RNA sequencing at 24 h under microaerobic fermentation conditions with an initial glucose of 40 g/l. The samples were sent to Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd for standardized next-generation RNA sequencing (Su et al. 2021 ).
Resuspend samples from frozen strain stocks and extract total RNA using the TRIzol method. Enrich Poly(A) mRNA using the NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Kit (NEB, E7490S). Fragment mRNA using NEBNext First-Strand Synthesis Buffer (NEB, E7525) with NEBNext Random Primers (NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina, NEB, E7335S). First-strand cDNA was synthesized using ProtoScript II reverse transcriptase (NEB, M0368X), followed by preparation of double-stranded cDNA via the Second Strand Synthesis Enzyme Mix (NEB, E7550S).
Double-stranded cDNA was purified using the AxyPrep Mag PCR Cleanup (Axygen, Union City, CA, USA) to purify double-stranded cDNA. End repair and dA tailing were performed using the End Prep Enzyme Mi

### Results and discussion
In previous studies, through EMS mutagenesis screening, we obtained a high-yielding isopentanol-producing evolutionary strain of S. cerevisiae , EMS39. Whole-genome resequencing results revealed significant variations in the coding and regulatory regions of the MSS11 gene in EMS39 compared to the original parental strain, specifically one missense mutation and six deletion mutations within the ORF (Su et al. 2021 ).
These results suggest that mutations in the MSS11 gene may be one of the key factors driving the metabolic phenotype changes (such as high isopentanol production) in the EMS39 strain, implying that MSS11 may play an important role in carbon metabolism flux allocation or secondary metabolic pathway regulation in S. cerevisiae . Based on this preliminary research clue, we speculate that functional abnormalities in MSS11 (including sequence mutations or changes in expression levels) may have widespread effects on the yeast’s overall metabolic network. Given that ethanol fermentation is a core industrial phenotype of S. cerevisiae , this study further focused on the regulatory effects of MSS11 overexpression on the ethanol fermentation process and conducted systematic experimental investigations.

### Ethanol fermentation in S. cerevisiae W303-1A (Eng-1 vs. Eng-0)
To assess the expression level of the MSS11 gene in the engineered strains, RT-qPCR was performed. This technique allows for the precise amplification and detection of specific DNA sequences in real time, providing accurate measurements of gene expression level (Ramos-Alonso et al. 2022 ). Total DNA was extracted from both the control strain (Eng-0) and the overexpression strain (Eng-1) at multiple time points during fermentation. During PCR amplification, fluorescent dyes were incorporated into the newly synthesized DNA strands, enabling real-time monitoring of amplification efficiency through fluorescence signal detection.
The results demonstrated that the MSS11 gene was successfully overexpressed in Eng-1, with expression levels 2.81-(corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.49), 2.55-(corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.35), and 2.33-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.22) higher than those in Eng-0 at 10, 24, and 28 h, respectively (Fig. 1 ). Statistical analysis using the two-tailed t -test confirmed that these increases were significant ( P &lt; 0.05), verifying the effectiveness of genetic modification.
Although the absolute increase in expression levels following MSS11 overexpression is relatively lower (2.30–2.83-fold, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.2–1.5), this is reasonable in S. cerevisiae overexpression system. Moreover, this aligns with the objective of this study to evaluate the phenotypic effects of overexpressing MSS11 at moderate and biologically relevant expression levels. Future studies may explore stronger expression systems to assess dose-dependent effects. As a transcriptional regulator rather than a structural gene, MSS11 is likely governed by intrinsic cellular feedback mechanisms; consequently, its overexpression could elicit pleiotropic stress responses within the cell. Therefore, moderate transcriptional upregulation aligns with the regulatory logic of yeast physiological metabolism and is a common phenomenon in the overexpression of such regu

### Differential gene expression analysis
A total of 178 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, with 136 genes up-regulated and 42 genes down-regulated in Eng-1 ( Tables S1 and S2 ). Figure 3 shows the volcano plot of DEGs between Eng-1 and Eng-0. These DEGs were functionally categorized using Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), and Eukaryotic Orthologous Groups (KOG) databases.

### GO enrichment analysis
GO analysis revealed that DEGs were significantly enriched in: cellular processes (e.g. cell wall organization, membrane integrity), metabolic pathways (e.g. carbohydrate metabolism, glycolysis), environmental stress responses (e.g. osmotic stress, oxidative stress) ( Fig. S1 ). Notably, the STD1 gene, which encodes a glucose-sensing regulatory protein (Tillman et al. 1995 ) was 5.54-fold increase (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.47) in Eng-1. This gene plays a crucial role in carbon catabolite repression, enabling cells to prioritize glucose utilization under varying nutrient conditions. Its overexpression likely contributed to the enhanced glycolytic flux observed in Eng-1, thereby boosting ethanol production.

### KEGG enrichment analysis
KEGG enrichment highlighted several key pathways (such as MAPK signaling pathway, carbon metabolism, mitochondrial energy metabolism, Fig. S2 ) influenced by MSS11 overexpression (Cheng et al. 2019 ). MAPK signaling pathway was critical for stress adaptation and metabolic regulation (Fig. 4a–b ). Moreover, as a downstream transcription regulator of the MAPK signaling pathway, MSS11 plays a crucial role in modulating stress response genes and metabolic genes (Fig. 4c ). The significant downregulation of the key gluconeogenesis gene FBP1 (2.87-fold, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.52) may create favorable conditions for carbon flow towards ethanol synthesis by reducing the reverse flux of carbon sources towards glucose. Although no clear upregulation of glycolytic genes was observed, the downregulation of FBP1 may represent one potential regulatory feature contributing to the reallocation of carbon flux towards ethanol synthesis. Enhanced expression of YBR238C (6.54-fold up, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.71) and SLS1 (4.35-fold up, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.12) improved ATP supply, supporting sustained fermentation under high ethanol concentrations (Sahana et al. 2024 ).

### Comprehensive analysis of metabolic reprogramming in engineered strains
Carbon metabolism remodeling enhances glycolytic flux

### Conclusion
To elucidate the molecular mechanism by which Eng-1 enhances ethanol production, we performed RNA-seq and compared the gene expression profiles of Eng-1 and Eng-0. The results showed that the expression of several key genes was altered, mainly affecting metabolic pathways, stress tolerance and global transcriptional reprogramming.
Firstly, the metabolic pathway STD1 gene was up-regulated by 5.54-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.47) to enhance glucose sensing and glycolysis efficiency, and FBP1 gene was down-regulated by 2.87-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.52) to reduce glycogen activity and shift carbon to ethanol synthesis. The MAE1 gene was upregulated 3.25-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.7) to increase the availability of pyruvate, a key precursor for ethanol fermentation. In addition, cellular resilience was enhanced, with activation of the MAPK pathway increasing resistance to ethanol toxicity and osmotic stress, ensuring sustained fermentation performance, and cell wall strengthening (e.g. BI4 gene, 1251.98-fold increase, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 10.29) enhancing membrane stability under high ethanol conditions. Also, for global transcriptional reprogramming, the FUS3 gene (2.68-fold increase, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.42) was a key regulator of the mating pathway, which may divert cellular resources from nonessential processes to fermentation; coordinated changes in the expression of transcription factors suggested that the MSS11 gene was a master regulator, integrating both metabolic and stress-response signals.
This work demonstrates that MSS11 overexpression significantly enhances ethanol production in S. cerevisiae through multi-level regulation of metabolism and stress adaptation. The strain-independent nature of this improvement, validated in both W303-1A and JT139, highlights its potential for industrial bioethanol production. ### Abstract
Bioethanol is a pivotal sustainable alternative to fossil fuels. Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the primary microorganism for its industrial production. Enhancing the fermentative performance of S. cerevisiae is crucial for sustainable bioethanol production. To systematically enhance the fermentative capacity of yeast, this study employed targeted genetic engineering to overexpress MSS11 -a principal transcription factor within the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling cascade. The resultant recombinant strain, Eng-1, demonstrated a marked 23.9% enhancement in final ethanol titer (18.94 g/l vs. 15.29 g/l) and a commensurate 23.8% improvement in yield coefficient (0.473 vs. 0.382 g ethanol per g glucose) relative to the isogenic control strain Eng-0 under microaerobic batch fermentation. This phenotype was consistently validated in a distinct genetic background (JT139 derivative), underscoring the generalizable function of MSS11 . Transcriptomic analysis revealed that MSS11 orchestrates a dual regulatory mechanism: it upregulates pyruvate-supplying pathway genes to enhance carbon flux toward ethanol, while concurrently activating a suite of genes involved in oxidative, osmotic, and ethanol stress tolerance to improve cellular robustness. These findings establish MSS11 as a novel and effective metabolic engineering target for yeast, and they elucidate its dual regulatory mechanism in coordinately enhancing carbon conversion and cellular robustness, thereby providing a strategic framework for constructing high-performance microbial cell factories for advanced biofuel production.
Keywords: Saccharomyces cerevisiae , ethanol, MSS11, transcriptome analysis, metabolic engineering

### Introduction
With society’s concern for environmental issues, biofuels are increasingly entering the production and living areas as partial substitutes for fossil fuels (Cherwoo et al. 2023 ). Bioethanol is an important biofuel processed from bioenergy sources such as rice husk (Gupte et al. 2022 ) and various microorganisms (Joyia et al. 2024 ). It has higher octane numbers, higher heat of vaporization, and lower vapor pressure, and is considered a clean, renewable and green combustible fuel that can replace gasoline. Studies have demonstrated that the use of bioethanol as a fuel can significantly improve engine performance and combustion characteristics (Thangavelu et al. 2016 , Mendiburu et al. 2022 ). In addition, ethanol is readily miscible and can be used as an oxidizing component in gasoline for cleaner emissions (Da Silva et al. 2019 ). Advantages of bioethanol over conventional fuels include better environmental sustainability of feedstock, lower greenhouse gas emissions, lower production costs, and more promising development prospects (Paluri and Patel 2022 ).
Bioethanol can be produced from different feedstocks, which can be broadly categorized into three groups: sucrose (Vaid et al. 2021 ), starch crops (Morais et al. 2019 ), and lignocellulosic biomass (Zabed et al. 2016 ). High price volatility and cost instability were observed for three different feedstocks (Tekin et al. 2018 ). Saccharomyces cerevisiae has a long history of being a microorganism with a favorable biosafety profile and is widely used in human production and life (Zhao et al. 2024 ). With the continuous progress of biotechnology, the increased demand for synthetic bioproducts and the requirements of the external environment have led to the continuous updating and optimization of S. cerevisiae strains. Through artificial cultivation and screening, more and more special-functioning S. cerevisiae strains have emerged from the wild type. Nowadays, S. cerevisiae is used not only in the food sector but a

### Strains and medium
The host strains selected for this work were S. cerevisiae W303-1A (Thomas and Rothstein 1989 ) and JT139 (Zhang 2009 ), and the genotypes associated with these strains are shown in Table 1 . Escherichia coli DH5α receptor cells were prepared in Luria–Bertani medium (1% tryptophan (w/v), 0.5% yeast paste, and 1% NaCl (w/v)) containing ampicillin for plasmid amplification. The yeast strains were maintained and propagated using YPD medium (2% peptone (w/v), 1% yeast extract (w/v) and 2% glucose (w/v). Complete limit medium [complete medium (CM), 2% glucose (w/v), 0.67% amino acid-free yeast nitrogen source (w/v), 0.83 g/l Dropout Powder, 0.1 g/l histidine, 0.1 g/l tryptophan, 0.1 g/l leucine, 0.05 g/l adenine, 0.05 g/l uracil] was used to screen the cells.

### Construction of plasmids and strains
The strains and plasmids used in this work are shown in Tables 1 and 2 . The MSS11 gene fragment was amplified by PCR using the specific primers MSS11 -U (5′-GGGCCCGAATTCGATACCGAATCACGAAGG-3′) and MSS11 -D (5′-GGGCCCGAATTCATAGTGTCACTGGCACCC-3′) with the genomic DNA of S. cerevisiae W303-1A as template. After Eco RI digestion, the fragment was ligated with YCplac22 vector (Gietz and Sugino 1988 ) by T 4 DNA ligase to successfully construct recombinant plasmid YCplac22- MSS11 .
Open in a new tab YCplac22 (control) and YCplac22- MSS11 (experimental group) were transformed into W303-1A and JT139 strains respectively by lithium acetate transformation. Successful transformants were selected on CM-Trp medium and verified by colony PCR. The primers MSS11 -U and MSS11 -D were designed to anneal within the MSS11
ORF itself. Crucially, this amplicon is present on both the chromosomal locus and the recombinant plasmid YCplac22- MSS11 . Therefore, a positive PCR signal confirms the presence of the MSS11 sequence in the cell but does not distinguish its genomic location. To unambiguously confirm the presence of the plasmid, we performed an additional control: only strains harboring the YCplac22-based plasmid (either empty or containing MSS11 ) can grow on CM-Trp medium, which provides direct phenotypic evidence of successful transformation. The specific overexpression of the MSS11 gene from the plasmid in the engineered strains was subsequently quantified and confirmed by real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis (Fig. 1 ), which measures the total MSS11 expression level and showed a significant increase in Eng-1 and Eng-3 compared to their respective controls

### Fermentation conditions and product determination
The fermentation process was conducted in three stages. First, an appropriate number of cells from the CM-Trp solid medium was inoculated into 5 ml of CM-Trp liquid medium for activation. After 2∼4 h, the cells were transferred into 45 ml of CM-Trp medium and incubated overnight at 30°C with continuous shaking at 200 rpm. Subsequently, the cells were inoculated into 100 ml of YPD medium for high-density fermentation, with the initial OD 600nm adjusted to 0.5. The initial glucose concentration was 40 g/l (4%(w/v)). During fermentation, samples were collected every 2 h to monitor cell growth and glucose consumption. Ethanol content in the fermentation broth was measured starting from the 10-h time point.
In the aforementioned shake flask fermentation experiment, microaerophilic conditions were employed. Add 100 milliliters of culture medium to a 250-ml fermentation flask, inoculate the culture, and then tightly sealed with aluminum foil (ensuring no gaps and allowing only minimal gas exchange). The fermentation bottles were then incubated in a shaking incubator at 30°C and 200 rpm. The initial air inside the shaking flasks was rapidly consumed during yeast growth and metabolism (especially during the initial aerobic respiration phase), while the tight sealing with aluminium foil significantly reduced the entry of external oxygen. After 6–8 h of fermentation, a low-oxygen environment gradually formed, thereby meeting the requirements for microaerobic fermentation.

### Transcriptomic sequencing
Transcriptome analysis is a comprehensive study of all transcriptional products within cells under specific conditions, primarily including mRNA, non-coding RNA, and other RNA species. In S. cerevisiae , transcriptome analysis is typically conducted using high-throughput sequencing technologies, such as RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). The main procedural steps are as follows: First, total RNA is extracted from yeast cells, and its concentration, purity, and integrity are assessed. The RNA is then fragmented and reverse transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA). Sequencing adapters are subsequently added to the cDNA, and the samples are sequenced using platforms such as Illumina HiSeq X Ten (San Diego, CA, USA). Finally, the sequencing data are processed through alignment, quantification, and differential expression analysis to identify and interpret transcriptional changes.
Transcriptome perturbations were analyzed for Eng-0 and Eng-1 strains. Eng-0 served as a control. Two RNA-Seq repeats were performed. Samples were collected for RNA sequencing at 24 h under microaerobic fermentation conditions with an initial glucose of 40 g/l. The samples were sent to Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd for standardized next-generation RNA sequencing (Su et al. 2021 ).
Resuspend samples from frozen strain stocks and extract total RNA using the TRIzol method. Enrich Poly(A) mRNA using the NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Kit (NEB, E7490S). Fragment mRNA using NEBNext First-Strand Synthesis Buffer (NEB, E7525) with NEBNext Random Primers (NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina, NEB, E7335S). First-strand cDNA was synthesized using ProtoScript II reverse transcriptase (NEB, M0368X), followed by preparation of double-stranded cDNA via the Second Strand Synthesis Enzyme Mix (NEB, E7550S).
Double-stranded cDNA was purified using the AxyPrep Mag PCR Cleanup (Axygen, Union City, CA, USA) to purify double-stranded cDNA. End repair and dA tailing were performed using the End Prep Enzyme Mi

### Results and discussion
In previous studies, through EMS mutagenesis screening, we obtained a high-yielding isopentanol-producing evolutionary strain of S. cerevisiae , EMS39. Whole-genome resequencing results revealed significant variations in the coding and regulatory regions of the MSS11 gene in EMS39 compared to the original parental strain, specifically one missense mutation and six deletion mutations within the ORF (Su et al. 2021 ).
These results suggest that mutations in the MSS11 gene may be one of the key factors driving the metabolic phenotype changes (such as high isopentanol production) in the EMS39 strain, implying that MSS11 may play an important role in carbon metabolism flux allocation or secondary metabolic pathway regulation in S. cerevisiae . Based on this preliminary research clue, we speculate that functional abnormalities in MSS11 (including sequence mutations or changes in expression levels) may have widespread effects on the yeast’s overall metabolic network. Given that ethanol fermentation is a core industrial phenotype of S. cerevisiae , this study further focused on the regulatory effects of MSS11 overexpression on the ethanol fermentation process and conducted systematic experimental investigations.

### Ethanol fermentation in S. cerevisiae W303-1A (Eng-1 vs. Eng-0)
To assess the expression level of the MSS11 gene in the engineered strains, RT-qPCR was performed. This technique allows for the precise amplification and detection of specific DNA sequences in real time, providing accurate measurements of gene expression level (Ramos-Alonso et al. 2022 ). Total DNA was extracted from both the control strain (Eng-0) and the overexpression strain (Eng-1) at multiple time points during fermentation. During PCR amplification, fluorescent dyes were incorporated into the newly synthesized DNA strands, enabling real-time monitoring of amplification efficiency through fluorescence signal detection.
The results demonstrated that the MSS11 gene was successfully overexpressed in Eng-1, with expression levels 2.81-(corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.49), 2.55-(corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.35), and 2.33-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.22) higher than those in Eng-0 at 10, 24, and 28 h, respectively (Fig. 1 ). Statistical analysis using the two-tailed t -test confirmed that these increases were significant ( P &lt; 0.05), verifying the effectiveness of genetic modification.
Although the absolute increase in expression levels following MSS11 overexpression is relatively lower (2.30–2.83-fold, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.2–1.5), this is reasonable in S. cerevisiae overexpression system. Moreover, this aligns with the objective of this study to evaluate the phenotypic effects of overexpressing MSS11 at moderate and biologically relevant expression levels. Future studies may explore stronger expression systems to assess dose-dependent effects. As a transcriptional regulator rather than a structural gene, MSS11 is likely governed by intrinsic cellular feedback mechanisms; consequently, its overexpression could elicit pleiotropic stress responses within the cell. Therefore, moderate transcriptional upregulation aligns with the regulatory logic of yeast physiological metabolism and is a common phenomenon in the overexpression of such regu

### Differential gene expression analysis
A total of 178 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, with 136 genes up-regulated and 42 genes down-regulated in Eng-1 ( Tables S1 and S2 ). Figure 3 shows the volcano plot of DEGs between Eng-1 and Eng-0. These DEGs were functionally categorized using Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), and Eukaryotic Orthologous Groups (KOG) databases.

### GO enrichment analysis
GO analysis revealed that DEGs were significantly enriched in: cellular processes (e.g. cell wall organization, membrane integrity), metabolic pathways (e.g. carbohydrate metabolism, glycolysis), environmental stress responses (e.g. osmotic stress, oxidative stress) ( Fig. S1 ). Notably, the STD1 gene, which encodes a glucose-sensing regulatory protein (Tillman et al. 1995 ) was 5.54-fold increase (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.47) in Eng-1. This gene plays a crucial role in carbon catabolite repression, enabling cells to prioritize glucose utilization under varying nutrient conditions. Its overexpression likely contributed to the enhanced glycolytic flux observed in Eng-1, thereby boosting ethanol production.

### KEGG enrichment analysis
KEGG enrichment highlighted several key pathways (such as MAPK signaling pathway, carbon metabolism, mitochondrial energy metabolism, Fig. S2 ) influenced by MSS11 overexpression (Cheng et al. 2019 ). MAPK signaling pathway was critical for stress adaptation and metabolic regulation (Fig. 4a–b ). Moreover, as a downstream transcription regulator of the MAPK signaling pathway, MSS11 plays a crucial role in modulating stress response genes and metabolic genes (Fig. 4c ). The significant downregulation of the key gluconeogenesis gene FBP1 (2.87-fold, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.52) may create favorable conditions for carbon flow towards ethanol synthesis by reducing the reverse flux of carbon sources towards glucose. Although no clear upregulation of glycolytic genes was observed, the downregulation of FBP1 may represent one potential regulatory feature contributing to the reallocation of carbon flux towards ethanol synthesis. Enhanced expression of YBR238C (6.54-fold up, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.71) and SLS1 (4.35-fold up, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.12) improved ATP supply, supporting sustained fermentation under high ethanol concentrations (Sahana et al. 2024 ).

### Comprehensive analysis of metabolic reprogramming in engineered strains
Carbon metabolism remodeling enhances glycolytic flux

### Conclusion
To elucidate the molecular mechanism by which Eng-1 enhances ethanol production, we performed RNA-seq and compared the gene expression profiles of Eng-1 and Eng-0. The results showed that the expression of several key genes was altered, mainly affecting metabolic pathways, stress tolerance and global transcriptional reprogramming.
Firstly, the metabolic pathway STD1 gene was up-regulated by 5.54-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.47) to enhance glucose sensing and glycolysis efficiency, and FBP1 gene was down-regulated by 2.87-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.52) to reduce glycogen activity and shift carbon to ethanol synthesis. The MAE1 gene was upregulated 3.25-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.7) to increase the availability of pyruvate, a key precursor for ethanol fermentation. In addition, cellular resilience was enhanced, with activation of the MAPK pathway increasing resistance to ethanol toxicity and osmotic stress, ensuring sustained fermentation performance, and cell wall strengthening (e.g. BI4 gene, 1251.98-fold increase, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 10.29) enhancing membrane stability under high ethanol conditions. Also, for global transcriptional reprogramming, the FUS3 gene (2.68-fold increase, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.42) was a key regulator of the mating pathway, which may divert cellular resources from nonessential processes to fermentation; coordinated changes in the expression of transcription factors suggested that the MSS11 gene was a master regulator, integrating both metabolic and stress-response signals.
This work demonstrates that MSS11 overexpression significantly enhances ethanol production in S. cerevisiae through multi-level regulation of metabolism and stress adaptation. The strain-independent nature of this improvement, validated in both W303-1A and JT139, highlights its potential for industrial bioethanol production. ### Abstract
Bioethanol is a pivotal sustainable alternative to fossil fuels. Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the primary microorganism for its industrial production. Enhancing the fermentative performance of S. cerevisiae is crucial for sustainable bioethanol production. To systematically enhance the fermentative capacity of yeast, this study employed targeted genetic engineering to overexpress MSS11 -a principal transcription factor within the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling cascade. The resultant recombinant strain, Eng-1, demonstrated a marked 23.9% enhancement in final ethanol titer (18.94 g/l vs. 15.29 g/l) and a commensurate 23.8% improvement in yield coefficient (0.473 vs. 0.382 g ethanol per g glucose) relative to the isogenic control strain Eng-0 under microaerobic batch fermentation. This phenotype was consistently validated in a distinct genetic background (JT139 derivative), underscoring the generalizable function of MSS11 . Transcriptomic analysis revealed that MSS11 orchestrates a dual regulatory mechanism: it upregulates pyruvate-supplying pathway genes to enhance carbon flux toward ethanol, while concurrently activating a suite of genes involved in oxidative, osmotic, and ethanol stress tolerance to improve cellular robustness. These findings establish MSS11 as a novel and effective metabolic engineering target for yeast, and they elucidate its dual regulatory mechanism in coordinately enhancing carbon conversion and cellular robustness, thereby providing a strategic framework for constructing high-performance microbial cell factories for advanced biofuel production.
Keywords: Saccharomyces cerevisiae , ethanol, MSS11, transcriptome analysis, metabolic engineering

### Introduction
With society’s concern for environmental issues, biofuels are increasingly entering the production and living areas as partial substitutes for fossil fuels (Cherwoo et al. 2023 ). Bioethanol is an important biofuel processed from bioenergy sources such as rice husk (Gupte et al. 2022 ) and various microorganisms (Joyia et al. 2024 ). It has higher octane numbers, higher heat of vaporization, and lower vapor pressure, and is considered a clean, renewable and green combustible fuel that can replace gasoline. Studies have demonstrated that the use of bioethanol as a fuel can significantly improve engine performance and combustion characteristics (Thangavelu et al. 2016 , Mendiburu et al. 2022 ). In addition, ethanol is readily miscible and can be used as an oxidizing component in gasoline for cleaner emissions (Da Silva et al. 2019 ). Advantages of bioethanol over conventional fuels include better environmental sustainability of feedstock, lower greenhouse gas emissions, lower production costs, and more promising development prospects (Paluri and Patel 2022 ).
Bioethanol can be produced from different feedstocks, which can be broadly categorized into three groups: sucrose (Vaid et al. 2021 ), starch crops (Morais et al. 2019 ), and lignocellulosic biomass (Zabed et al. 2016 ). High price volatility and cost instability were observed for three different feedstocks (Tekin et al. 2018 ). Saccharomyces cerevisiae has a long history of being a microorganism with a favorable biosafety profile and is widely used in human production and life (Zhao et al. 2024 ). With the continuous progress of biotechnology, the increased demand for synthetic bioproducts and the requirements of the external environment have led to the continuous updating and optimization of S. cerevisiae strains. Through artificial cultivation and screening, more and more special-functioning S. cerevisiae strains have emerged from the wild type. Nowadays, S. cerevisiae is used not only in the food sector but a

### Strains and medium
The host strains selected for this work were S. cerevisiae W303-1A (Thomas and Rothstein 1989 ) and JT139 (Zhang 2009 ), and the genotypes associated with these strains are shown in Table 1 . Escherichia coli DH5α receptor cells were prepared in Luria–Bertani medium (1% tryptophan (w/v), 0.5% yeast paste, and 1% NaCl (w/v)) containing ampicillin for plasmid amplification. The yeast strains were maintained and propagated using YPD medium (2% peptone (w/v), 1% yeast extract (w/v) and 2% glucose (w/v). Complete limit medium [complete medium (CM), 2% glucose (w/v), 0.67% amino acid-free yeast nitrogen source (w/v), 0.83 g/l Dropout Powder, 0.1 g/l histidine, 0.1 g/l tryptophan, 0.1 g/l leucine, 0.05 g/l adenine, 0.05 g/l uracil] was used to screen the cells.

### Construction of plasmids and strains
The strains and plasmids used in this work are shown in Tables 1 and 2 . The MSS11 gene fragment was amplified by PCR using the specific primers MSS11 -U (5′-GGGCCCGAATTCGATACCGAATCACGAAGG-3′) and MSS11 -D (5′-GGGCCCGAATTCATAGTGTCACTGGCACCC-3′) with the genomic DNA of S. cerevisiae W303-1A as template. After Eco RI digestion, the fragment was ligated with YCplac22 vector (Gietz and Sugino 1988 ) by T 4 DNA ligase to successfully construct recombinant plasmid YCplac22- MSS11 .
Open in a new tab YCplac22 (control) and YCplac22- MSS11 (experimental group) were transformed into W303-1A and JT139 strains respectively by lithium acetate transformation. Successful transformants were selected on CM-Trp medium and verified by colony PCR. The primers MSS11 -U and MSS11 -D were designed to anneal within the MSS11
ORF itself. Crucially, this amplicon is present on both the chromosomal locus and the recombinant plasmid YCplac22- MSS11 . Therefore, a positive PCR signal confirms the presence of the MSS11 sequence in the cell but does not distinguish its genomic location. To unambiguously confirm the presence of the plasmid, we performed an additional control: only strains harboring the YCplac22-based plasmid (either empty or containing MSS11 ) can grow on CM-Trp medium, which provides direct phenotypic evidence of successful transformation. The specific overexpression of the MSS11 gene from the plasmid in the engineered strains was subsequently quantified and confirmed by real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis (Fig. 1 ), which measures the total MSS11 expression level and showed a significant increase in Eng-1 and Eng-3 compared to their respective controls

### Fermentation conditions and product determination
The fermentation process was conducted in three stages. First, an appropriate number of cells from the CM-Trp solid medium was inoculated into 5 ml of CM-Trp liquid medium for activation. After 2∼4 h, the cells were transferred into 45 ml of CM-Trp medium and incubated overnight at 30°C with continuous shaking at 200 rpm. Subsequently, the cells were inoculated into 100 ml of YPD medium for high-density fermentation, with the initial OD 600nm adjusted to 0.5. The initial glucose concentration was 40 g/l (4%(w/v)). During fermentation, samples were collected every 2 h to monitor cell growth and glucose consumption. Ethanol content in the fermentation broth was measured starting from the 10-h time point.
In the aforementioned shake flask fermentation experiment, microaerophilic conditions were employed. Add 100 milliliters of culture medium to a 250-ml fermentation flask, inoculate the culture, and then tightly sealed with aluminum foil (ensuring no gaps and allowing only minimal gas exchange). The fermentation bottles were then incubated in a shaking incubator at 30°C and 200 rpm. The initial air inside the shaking flasks was rapidly consumed during yeast growth and metabolism (especially during the initial aerobic respiration phase), while the tight sealing with aluminium foil significantly reduced the entry of external oxygen. After 6–8 h of fermentation, a low-oxygen environment gradually formed, thereby meeting the requirements for microaerobic fermentation.

### Transcriptomic sequencing
Transcriptome analysis is a comprehensive study of all transcriptional products within cells under specific conditions, primarily including mRNA, non-coding RNA, and other RNA species. In S. cerevisiae , transcriptome analysis is typically conducted using high-throughput sequencing technologies, such as RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). The main procedural steps are as follows: First, total RNA is extracted from yeast cells, and its concentration, purity, and integrity are assessed. The RNA is then fragmented and reverse transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA). Sequencing adapters are subsequently added to the cDNA, and the samples are sequenced using platforms such as Illumina HiSeq X Ten (San Diego, CA, USA). Finally, the sequencing data are processed through alignment, quantification, and differential expression analysis to identify and interpret transcriptional changes.
Transcriptome perturbations were analyzed for Eng-0 and Eng-1 strains. Eng-0 served as a control. Two RNA-Seq repeats were performed. Samples were collected for RNA sequencing at 24 h under microaerobic fermentation conditions with an initial glucose of 40 g/l. The samples were sent to Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd for standardized next-generation RNA sequencing (Su et al. 2021 ).
Resuspend samples from frozen strain stocks and extract total RNA using the TRIzol method. Enrich Poly(A) mRNA using the NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Kit (NEB, E7490S). Fragment mRNA using NEBNext First-Strand Synthesis Buffer (NEB, E7525) with NEBNext Random Primers (NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina, NEB, E7335S). First-strand cDNA was synthesized using ProtoScript II reverse transcriptase (NEB, M0368X), followed by preparation of double-stranded cDNA via the Second Strand Synthesis Enzyme Mix (NEB, E7550S).
Double-stranded cDNA was purified using the AxyPrep Mag PCR Cleanup (Axygen, Union City, CA, USA) to purify double-stranded cDNA. End repair and dA tailing were performed using the End Prep Enzyme Mi

### Results and discussion
In previous studies, through EMS mutagenesis screening, we obtained a high-yielding isopentanol-producing evolutionary strain of S. cerevisiae , EMS39. Whole-genome resequencing results revealed significant variations in the coding and regulatory regions of the MSS11 gene in EMS39 compared to the original parental strain, specifically one missense mutation and six deletion mutations within the ORF (Su et al. 2021 ).
These results suggest that mutations in the MSS11 gene may be one of the key factors driving the metabolic phenotype changes (such as high isopentanol production) in the EMS39 strain, implying that MSS11 may play an important role in carbon metabolism flux allocation or secondary metabolic pathway regulation in S. cerevisiae . Based on this preliminary research clue, we speculate that functional abnormalities in MSS11 (including sequence mutations or changes in expression levels) may have widespread effects on the yeast’s overall metabolic network. Given that ethanol fermentation is a core industrial phenotype of S. cerevisiae , this study further focused on the regulatory effects of MSS11 overexpression on the ethanol fermentation process and conducted systematic experimental investigations.

### Ethanol fermentation in S. cerevisiae W303-1A (Eng-1 vs. Eng-0)
To assess the expression level of the MSS11 gene in the engineered strains, RT-qPCR was performed. This technique allows for the precise amplification and detection of specific DNA sequences in real time, providing accurate measurements of gene expression level (Ramos-Alonso et al. 2022 ). Total DNA was extracted from both the control strain (Eng-0) and the overexpression strain (Eng-1) at multiple time points during fermentation. During PCR amplification, fluorescent dyes were incorporated into the newly synthesized DNA strands, enabling real-time monitoring of amplification efficiency through fluorescence signal detection.
The results demonstrated that the MSS11 gene was successfully overexpressed in Eng-1, with expression levels 2.81-(corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.49), 2.55-(corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.35), and 2.33-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.22) higher than those in Eng-0 at 10, 24, and 28 h, respectively (Fig. 1 ). Statistical analysis using the two-tailed t -test confirmed that these increases were significant ( P &lt; 0.05), verifying the effectiveness of genetic modification.
Although the absolute increase in expression levels following MSS11 overexpression is relatively lower (2.30–2.83-fold, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.2–1.5), this is reasonable in S. cerevisiae overexpression system. Moreover, this aligns with the objective of this study to evaluate the phenotypic effects of overexpressing MSS11 at moderate and biologically relevant expression levels. Future studies may explore stronger expression systems to assess dose-dependent effects. As a transcriptional regulator rather than a structural gene, MSS11 is likely governed by intrinsic cellular feedback mechanisms; consequently, its overexpression could elicit pleiotropic stress responses within the cell. Therefore, moderate transcriptional upregulation aligns with the regulatory logic of yeast physiological metabolism and is a common phenomenon in the overexpression of such regu

### Differential gene expression analysis
A total of 178 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, with 136 genes up-regulated and 42 genes down-regulated in Eng-1 ( Tables S1 and S2 ). Figure 3 shows the volcano plot of DEGs between Eng-1 and Eng-0. These DEGs were functionally categorized using Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), and Eukaryotic Orthologous Groups (KOG) databases.

### GO enrichment analysis
GO analysis revealed that DEGs were significantly enriched in: cellular processes (e.g. cell wall organization, membrane integrity), metabolic pathways (e.g. carbohydrate metabolism, glycolysis), environmental stress responses (e.g. osmotic stress, oxidative stress) ( Fig. S1 ). Notably, the STD1 gene, which encodes a glucose-sensing regulatory protein (Tillman et al. 1995 ) was 5.54-fold increase (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.47) in Eng-1. This gene plays a crucial role in carbon catabolite repression, enabling cells to prioritize glucose utilization under varying nutrient conditions. Its overexpression likely contributed to the enhanced glycolytic flux observed in Eng-1, thereby boosting ethanol production.

### KEGG enrichment analysis
KEGG enrichment highlighted several key pathways (such as MAPK signaling pathway, carbon metabolism, mitochondrial energy metabolism, Fig. S2 ) influenced by MSS11 overexpression (Cheng et al. 2019 ). MAPK signaling pathway was critical for stress adaptation and metabolic regulation (Fig. 4a–b ). Moreover, as a downstream transcription regulator of the MAPK signaling pathway, MSS11 plays a crucial role in modulating stress response genes and metabolic genes (Fig. 4c ). The significant downregulation of the key gluconeogenesis gene FBP1 (2.87-fold, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.52) may create favorable conditions for carbon flow towards ethanol synthesis by reducing the reverse flux of carbon sources towards glucose. Although no clear upregulation of glycolytic genes was observed, the downregulation of FBP1 may represent one potential regulatory feature contributing to the reallocation of carbon flux towards ethanol synthesis. Enhanced expression of YBR238C (6.54-fold up, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.71) and SLS1 (4.35-fold up, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.12) improved ATP supply, supporting sustained fermentation under high ethanol concentrations (Sahana et al. 2024 ).

### Comprehensive analysis of metabolic reprogramming in engineered strains
Carbon metabolism remodeling enhances glycolytic flux

### Conclusion
To elucidate the molecular mechanism by which Eng-1 enhances ethanol production, we performed RNA-seq and compared the gene expression profiles of Eng-1 and Eng-0. The results showed that the expression of several key genes was altered, mainly affecting metabolic pathways, stress tolerance and global transcriptional reprogramming.
Firstly, the metabolic pathway STD1 gene was up-regulated by 5.54-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.47) to enhance glucose sensing and glycolysis efficiency, and FBP1 gene was down-regulated by 2.87-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.52) to reduce glycogen activity and shift carbon to ethanol synthesis. The MAE1 gene was upregulated 3.25-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.7) to increase the availability of pyruvate, a key precursor for ethanol fermentation. In addition, cellular resilience was enhanced, with activation of the MAPK pathway increasing resistance to ethanol toxicity and osmotic stress, ensuring sustained fermentation performance, and cell wall strengthening (e.g. BI4 gene, 1251.98-fold increase, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 10.29) enhancing membrane stability under high ethanol conditions. Also, for global transcriptional reprogramming, the FUS3 gene (2.68-fold increase, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.42) was a key regulator of the mating pathway, which may divert cellular resources from nonessential processes to fermentation; coordinated changes in the expression of transcription factors suggested that the MSS11 gene was a master regulator, integrating both metabolic and stress-response signals.
This work demonstrates that MSS11 overexpression significantly enhances ethanol production in S. cerevisiae through multi-level regulation of metabolism and stress adaptation. The strain-independent nature of this improvement, validated in both W303-1A and JT139, highlights its potential for industrial bioethanol production. ### Abstract
Bioethanol is a pivotal sustainable alternative to fossil fuels. Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the primary microorganism for its industrial production. Enhancing the fermentative performance of S. cerevisiae is crucial for sustainable bioethanol production. To systematically enhance the fermentative capacity of yeast, this study employed targeted genetic engineering to overexpress MSS11 -a principal transcription factor within the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling cascade. The resultant recombinant strain, Eng-1, demonstrated a marked 23.9% enhancement in final ethanol titer (18.94 g/l vs. 15.29 g/l) and a commensurate 23.8% improvement in yield coefficient (0.473 vs. 0.382 g ethanol per g glucose) relative to the isogenic control strain Eng-0 under microaerobic batch fermentation. This phenotype was consistently validated in a distinct genetic background (JT139 derivative), underscoring the generalizable function of MSS11 . Transcriptomic analysis revealed that MSS11 orchestrates a dual regulatory mechanism: it upregulates pyruvate-supplying pathway genes to enhance carbon flux toward ethanol, while concurrently activating a suite of genes involved in oxidative, osmotic, and ethanol stress tolerance to improve cellular robustness. These findings establish MSS11 as a novel and effective metabolic engineering target for yeast, and they elucidate its dual regulatory mechanism in coordinately enhancing carbon conversion and cellular robustness, thereby providing a strategic framework for constructing high-performance microbial cell factories for advanced biofuel production.
Keywords: Saccharomyces cerevisiae , ethanol, MSS11, transcriptome analysis, metabolic engineering

### Introduction
With society’s concern for environmental issues, biofuels are increasingly entering the production and living areas as partial substitutes for fossil fuels (Cherwoo et al. 2023 ). Bioethanol is an important biofuel processed from bioenergy sources such as rice husk (Gupte et al. 2022 ) and various microorganisms (Joyia et al. 2024 ). It has higher octane numbers, higher heat of vaporization, and lower vapor pressure, and is considered a clean, renewable and green combustible fuel that can replace gasoline. Studies have demonstrated that the use of bioethanol as a fuel can significantly improve engine performance and combustion characteristics (Thangavelu et al. 2016 , Mendiburu et al. 2022 ). In addition, ethanol is readily miscible and can be used as an oxidizing component in gasoline for cleaner emissions (Da Silva et al. 2019 ). Advantages of bioethanol over conventional fuels include better environmental sustainability of feedstock, lower greenhouse gas emissions, lower production costs, and more promising development prospects (Paluri and Patel 2022 ).
Bioethanol can be produced from different feedstocks, which can be broadly categorized into three groups: sucrose (Vaid et al. 2021 ), starch crops (Morais et al. 2019 ), and lignocellulosic biomass (Zabed et al. 2016 ). High price volatility and cost instability were observed for three different feedstocks (Tekin et al. 2018 ). Saccharomyces cerevisiae has a long history of being a microorganism with a favorable biosafety profile and is widely used in human production and life (Zhao et al. 2024 ). With the continuous progress of biotechnology, the increased demand for synthetic bioproducts and the requirements of the external environment have led to the continuous updating and optimization of S. cerevisiae strains. Through artificial cultivation and screening, more and more special-functioning S. cerevisiae strains have emerged from the wild type. Nowadays, S. cerevisiae is used not only in the food sector but a

### Strains and medium
The host strains selected for this work were S. cerevisiae W303-1A (Thomas and Rothstein 1989 ) and JT139 (Zhang 2009 ), and the genotypes associated with these strains are shown in Table 1 . Escherichia coli DH5α receptor cells were prepared in Luria–Bertani medium (1% tryptophan (w/v), 0.5% yeast paste, and 1% NaCl (w/v)) containing ampicillin for plasmid amplification. The yeast strains were maintained and propagated using YPD medium (2% peptone (w/v), 1% yeast extract (w/v) and 2% glucose (w/v). Complete limit medium [complete medium (CM), 2% glucose (w/v), 0.67% amino acid-free yeast nitrogen source (w/v), 0.83 g/l Dropout Powder, 0.1 g/l histidine, 0.1 g/l tryptophan, 0.1 g/l leucine, 0.05 g/l adenine, 0.05 g/l uracil] was used to screen the cells.

### Construction of plasmids and strains
The strains and plasmids used in this work are shown in Tables 1 and 2 . The MSS11 gene fragment was amplified by PCR using the specific primers MSS11 -U (5′-GGGCCCGAATTCGATACCGAATCACGAAGG-3′) and MSS11 -D (5′-GGGCCCGAATTCATAGTGTCACTGGCACCC-3′) with the genomic DNA of S. cerevisiae W303-1A as template. After Eco RI digestion, the fragment was ligated with YCplac22 vector (Gietz and Sugino 1988 ) by T 4 DNA ligase to successfully construct recombinant plasmid YCplac22- MSS11 .
Open in a new tab YCplac22 (control) and YCplac22- MSS11 (experimental group) were transformed into W303-1A and JT139 strains respectively by lithium acetate transformation. Successful transformants were selected on CM-Trp medium and verified by colony PCR. The primers MSS11 -U and MSS11 -D were designed to anneal within the MSS11
ORF itself. Crucially, this amplicon is present on both the chromosomal locus and the recombinant plasmid YCplac22- MSS11 . Therefore, a positive PCR signal confirms the presence of the MSS11 sequence in the cell but does not distinguish its genomic location. To unambiguously confirm the presence of the plasmid, we performed an additional control: only strains harboring the YCplac22-based plasmid (either empty or containing MSS11 ) can grow on CM-Trp medium, which provides direct phenotypic evidence of successful transformation. The specific overexpression of the MSS11 gene from the plasmid in the engineered strains was subsequently quantified and confirmed by real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis (Fig. 1 ), which measures the total MSS11 expression level and showed a significant increase in Eng-1 and Eng-3 compared to their respective controls

### Fermentation conditions and product determination
The fermentation process was conducted in three stages. First, an appropriate number of cells from the CM-Trp solid medium was inoculated into 5 ml of CM-Trp liquid medium for activation. After 2∼4 h, the cells were transferred into 45 ml of CM-Trp medium and incubated overnight at 30°C with continuous shaking at 200 rpm. Subsequently, the cells were inoculated into 100 ml of YPD medium for high-density fermentation, with the initial OD 600nm adjusted to 0.5. The initial glucose concentration was 40 g/l (4%(w/v)). During fermentation, samples were collected every 2 h to monitor cell growth and glucose consumption. Ethanol content in the fermentation broth was measured starting from the 10-h time point.
In the aforementioned shake flask fermentation experiment, microaerophilic conditions were employed. Add 100 milliliters of culture medium to a 250-ml fermentation flask, inoculate the culture, and then tightly sealed with aluminum foil (ensuring no gaps and allowing only minimal gas exchange). The fermentation bottles were then incubated in a shaking incubator at 30°C and 200 rpm. The initial air inside the shaking flasks was rapidly consumed during yeast growth and metabolism (especially during the initial aerobic respiration phase), while the tight sealing with aluminium foil significantly reduced the entry of external oxygen. After 6–8 h of fermentation, a low-oxygen environment gradually formed, thereby meeting the requirements for microaerobic fermentation.

### Transcriptomic sequencing
Transcriptome analysis is a comprehensive study of all transcriptional products within cells under specific conditions, primarily including mRNA, non-coding RNA, and other RNA species. In S. cerevisiae , transcriptome analysis is typically conducted using high-throughput sequencing technologies, such as RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). The main procedural steps are as follows: First, total RNA is extracted from yeast cells, and its concentration, purity, and integrity are assessed. The RNA is then fragmented and reverse transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA). Sequencing adapters are subsequently added to the cDNA, and the samples are sequenced using platforms such as Illumina HiSeq X Ten (San Diego, CA, USA). Finally, the sequencing data are processed through alignment, quantification, and differential expression analysis to identify and interpret transcriptional changes.
Transcriptome perturbations were analyzed for Eng-0 and Eng-1 strains. Eng-0 served as a control. Two RNA-Seq repeats were performed. Samples were collected for RNA sequencing at 24 h under microaerobic fermentation conditions with an initial glucose of 40 g/l. The samples were sent to Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd for standardized next-generation RNA sequencing (Su et al. 2021 ).
Resuspend samples from frozen strain stocks and extract total RNA using the TRIzol method. Enrich Poly(A) mRNA using the NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Kit (NEB, E7490S). Fragment mRNA using NEBNext First-Strand Synthesis Buffer (NEB, E7525) with NEBNext Random Primers (NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina, NEB, E7335S). First-strand cDNA was synthesized using ProtoScript II reverse transcriptase (NEB, M0368X), followed by preparation of double-stranded cDNA via the Second Strand Synthesis Enzyme Mix (NEB, E7550S).
Double-stranded cDNA was purified using the AxyPrep Mag PCR Cleanup (Axygen, Union City, CA, USA) to purify double-stranded cDNA. End repair and dA tailing were performed using the End Prep Enzyme Mi

### Results and discussion
In previous studies, through EMS mutagenesis screening, we obtained a high-yielding isopentanol-producing evolutionary strain of S. cerevisiae , EMS39. Whole-genome resequencing results revealed significant variations in the coding and regulatory regions of the MSS11 gene in EMS39 compared to the original parental strain, specifically one missense mutation and six deletion mutations within the ORF (Su et al. 2021 ).
These results suggest that mutations in the MSS11 gene may be one of the key factors driving the metabolic phenotype changes (such as high isopentanol production) in the EMS39 strain, implying that MSS11 may play an important role in carbon metabolism flux allocation or secondary metabolic pathway regulation in S. cerevisiae . Based on this preliminary research clue, we speculate that functional abnormalities in MSS11 (including sequence mutations or changes in expression levels) may have widespread effects on the yeast’s overall metabolic network. Given that ethanol fermentation is a core industrial phenotype of S. cerevisiae , this study further focused on the regulatory effects of MSS11 overexpression on the ethanol fermentation process and conducted systematic experimental investigations.

### Ethanol fermentation in S. cerevisiae W303-1A (Eng-1 vs. Eng-0)
To assess the expression level of the MSS11 gene in the engineered strains, RT-qPCR was performed. This technique allows for the precise amplification and detection of specific DNA sequences in real time, providing accurate measurements of gene expression level (Ramos-Alonso et al. 2022 ). Total DNA was extracted from both the control strain (Eng-0) and the overexpression strain (Eng-1) at multiple time points during fermentation. During PCR amplification, fluorescent dyes were incorporated into the newly synthesized DNA strands, enabling real-time monitoring of amplification efficiency through fluorescence signal detection.
The results demonstrated that the MSS11 gene was successfully overexpressed in Eng-1, with expression levels 2.81-(corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.49), 2.55-(corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.35), and 2.33-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.22) higher than those in Eng-0 at 10, 24, and 28 h, respectively (Fig. 1 ). Statistical analysis using the two-tailed t -test confirmed that these increases were significant ( P &lt; 0.05), verifying the effectiveness of genetic modification.
Although the absolute increase in expression levels following MSS11 overexpression is relatively lower (2.30–2.83-fold, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.2–1.5), this is reasonable in S. cerevisiae overexpression system. Moreover, this aligns with the objective of this study to evaluate the phenotypic effects of overexpressing MSS11 at moderate and biologically relevant expression levels. Future studies may explore stronger expression systems to assess dose-dependent effects. As a transcriptional regulator rather than a structural gene, MSS11 is likely governed by intrinsic cellular feedback mechanisms; consequently, its overexpression could elicit pleiotropic stress responses within the cell. Therefore, moderate transcriptional upregulation aligns with the regulatory logic of yeast physiological metabolism and is a common phenomenon in the overexpression of such regu

### Differential gene expression analysis
A total of 178 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, with 136 genes up-regulated and 42 genes down-regulated in Eng-1 ( Tables S1 and S2 ). Figure 3 shows the volcano plot of DEGs between Eng-1 and Eng-0. These DEGs were functionally categorized using Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), and Eukaryotic Orthologous Groups (KOG) databases.

### GO enrichment analysis
GO analysis revealed that DEGs were significantly enriched in: cellular processes (e.g. cell wall organization, membrane integrity), metabolic pathways (e.g. carbohydrate metabolism, glycolysis), environmental stress responses (e.g. osmotic stress, oxidative stress) ( Fig. S1 ). Notably, the STD1 gene, which encodes a glucose-sensing regulatory protein (Tillman et al. 1995 ) was 5.54-fold increase (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.47) in Eng-1. This gene plays a crucial role in carbon catabolite repression, enabling cells to prioritize glucose utilization under varying nutrient conditions. Its overexpression likely contributed to the enhanced glycolytic flux observed in Eng-1, thereby boosting ethanol production.

### KEGG enrichment analysis
KEGG enrichment highlighted several key pathways (such as MAPK signaling pathway, carbon metabolism, mitochondrial energy metabolism, Fig. S2 ) influenced by MSS11 overexpression (Cheng et al. 2019 ). MAPK signaling pathway was critical for stress adaptation and metabolic regulation (Fig. 4a–b ). Moreover, as a downstream transcription regulator of the MAPK signaling pathway, MSS11 plays a crucial role in modulating stress response genes and metabolic genes (Fig. 4c ). The significant downregulation of the key gluconeogenesis gene FBP1 (2.87-fold, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.52) may create favorable conditions for carbon flow towards ethanol synthesis by reducing the reverse flux of carbon sources towards glucose. Although no clear upregulation of glycolytic genes was observed, the downregulation of FBP1 may represent one potential regulatory feature contributing to the reallocation of carbon flux towards ethanol synthesis. Enhanced expression of YBR238C (6.54-fold up, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.71) and SLS1 (4.35-fold up, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.12) improved ATP supply, supporting sustained fermentation under high ethanol concentrations (Sahana et al. 2024 ).

### Comprehensive analysis of metabolic reprogramming in engineered strains
Carbon metabolism remodeling enhances glycolytic flux

### Conclusion
To elucidate the molecular mechanism by which Eng-1 enhances ethanol production, we performed RNA-seq and compared the gene expression profiles of Eng-1 and Eng-0. The results showed that the expression of several key genes was altered, mainly affecting metabolic pathways, stress tolerance and global transcriptional reprogramming.
Firstly, the metabolic pathway STD1 gene was up-regulated by 5.54-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 2.47) to enhance glucose sensing and glycolysis efficiency, and FBP1 gene was down-regulated by 2.87-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.52) to reduce glycogen activity and shift carbon to ethanol synthesis. The MAE1 gene was upregulated 3.25-fold (corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.7) to increase the availability of pyruvate, a key precursor for ethanol fermentation. In addition, cellular resilience was enhanced, with activation of the MAPK pathway increasing resistance to ethanol toxicity and osmotic stress, ensuring sustained fermentation performance, and cell wall strengthening (e.g. BI4 gene, 1251.98-fold increase, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 10.29) enhancing membrane stability under high ethanol conditions. Also, for global transcriptional reprogramming, the FUS3 gene (2.68-fold increase, corresponding to a log 2 FC of 1.42) was a key regulator of the mating pathway, which may divert cellular resources from nonessential processes to fermentation; coordinated changes in the expression of transcription factors suggested that the MSS11 gene was a master regulator, integrating both metabolic and stress-response signals.
This work demonstrates that MSS11 overexpression significantly enhances ethanol production in S. cerevisiae through multi-level regulation of metabolism and stress adaptation. The strain-independent nature of this improvement, validated in both W303-1A and JT139, highlights its potential for industrial bioethanol production. ### Abstract
Bioethanol is a pivotal sustainable alternative to fossil fuels. Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the primary microorganism for its industrial production. Enhancing the fermentative performance of S. cerevisiae is crucial for sustainable bioethanol production. To systematically enhance the fermentative capacity of yeast, this study employed targeted genetic engineering to overexpress MSS11 -a principal transcription factor within the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling cascade. The resultant recombinant strain, Eng-1, demonstrated a marked 23.9% enhancement in final ethanol titer (18.94 g/l vs. 15.29 g/l) and a commensurate 23.8% improvement in yield coefficient (0.473 vs. 0.382 g ethanol per g glucose) relative to the isogenic control strain Eng-0 under microaerobic batch fermentation. This phenotype was consistently validated in a distinct genetic background (JT139 derivative), underscoring the generalizable function of MSS11 . Transcriptomic analysis revealed that MSS11 orchestrates a dual regulatory mechanism: it upregulates pyruvate-supplying pathway genes to enhance carbon flux toward ethanol, while concurrently activating a suite of genes involved in oxidative, osmotic, and ethanol stress tolerance to improve cellular robustness. These findings establish MSS11 as a novel and effective metabolic engineering target for yeast, and they elucidate its dual regulatory mechanism in coordinately enhancing carbon conversion and cellular robustness, thereby providing a strategic framework for constructing high-performance microbial cell factories for advanced biofuel production.
Keywords: Saccharomyces cerevisiae , ethanol, MSS11, transcriptome analysis, metabolic engineering

### Introduction
With society’s concern for environmental issues, biofuels are increasingly entering the production and living areas as partial substitutes for fossil fuels (Cherwoo et al. 2023 ). Bioethanol is an important biofuel processed from bioenergy sources such as rice husk (Gupte et al. 2022 ) and various microorganisms (Joyia et al. 2024 ). It has higher octane numbers, higher heat of vaporization, and lower vapor pressure, and is considered a clean, renewable and green combustible fuel that can replace gasoline. Studies have demonstrated that the use of bioethanol as a fuel can significantly improve engine performance and combustion characteristics (Thangavelu et al. 2016 , Mendiburu et al. 2022 ). In addition, ethanol is readily miscible and can be used as an oxidizing component in gasoline for cleaner emissions (Da Silva et al. 2019 ). Advantages of bioethanol over conventional fuels include better environmental sustainability of feedstock, lower greenhouse gas emissions, lower production costs, and more promising development prospects (Paluri and Patel 2022 ).
Bioethanol can be produced from different feedstocks, which can be broadly categorized into three groups: sucrose (Vaid et al. 2021 ), starch crops (Morais et al. 2019 ), and lignocellulosic biomass (Zabed et al. 2016 ). High price volatility and cost instability were observed for three different feedstocks (Tekin et al. 2018 ). Saccharomyces cerevisiae has a long history of being a microorganism with a favorable biosafety profile and is widely used in human production and life (Zhao et al. 2024 ). With the continuous progress of biotechnology, the increased demand for synthetic bioproducts and the requirements of the external environment have led to the continuous updating and optimization of S. cerevisiae strains. Through artificial cultivation and screening, more and more special-functioning S. cerevisiae strains have emerged from the wild type. Nowadays, S. cerevisiae is used not only in the food sector but a

### Strains and medium
The host strains selected for this work were S. cerevisiae W303-1A (Thomas and Rothstein 1989 ) and JT139 (Zhang 2009 ), and the genotypes associated with these strains are shown in Table 1 . Escherichia coli DH5α receptor cells were prepared in Luria–Bertani medium (1% tryptophan (w/v), 0.5% yeast paste, and 1% NaCl (w/v)) containing ampicillin for plasmid amplification. The yeast strains were maintained and propagated using YPD medium (2% peptone (w/v), 1% yeast extract (w/v) and 2% glucose (w/v). Complete limit medium [complete medium (CM), 2% glucose (w/v), 0.67% amino acid-free yeast nitrogen source (w/v), 0.83 g/l Dropout Powder, 0.1 g/l histidine, 0.1 g/l tryptophan, 0.1 g/l leucine, 0.05 g/l adenine, 0.05 g/l uracil] was used to screen the cells.
